extracted.intended_audience: educated general readership; listeners/readers of 19th-century lectures on history, literature, and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for recognizing, evaluating, and understanding 'Heroes' and the King/Able-man in history and literature, as presented in a Victorian lecture. Emphasizes moral qualities, practical capacity, sincerity, and social effects of heroism and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverence for Excellence / Hero-worship
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine reverence or 'worship' for excellence is proper and valuable — exemplified by Boswell's awe of Johnson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hero-worship is a social necessity: it marks recognition of true excellence and provides moral and cultural orientation. Anti-pattern: those closest (the valet-de-chambre) often fail to recognize a Hero; worship misplaced on shallow figures is a societal problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural Nobleness / Symmetrical Completeness (as a mark of excellence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works or personalities of the highest order possess an 'architectural nobleness'—a sense of finished, symmetrical completeness, indicating a true Builder behind them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied metaphorically (e.g., Johnson's Dictionary): judge greatness by the solidity, completeness, and craft showing a guiding principle. Examples: Johnson's work stands like a 'great solid square-built edifice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Steadiness / Guidance amid Chaos
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hero guides a difficult, confused existence wisely; they have a 'loadstar' (moral compass) and will not change course in worldly vortices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the person preserves integrity and direction despite poverty, disorder, or chaos (Johnson as example). Anti-pattern: surrendering principles to expediency, 'striking the flag' before destructive forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Strength vs. Mere Vehemence
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength is calm endurance and the capacity to hold peace until the right time to speak or act; vehemence, convulsive fits, and spasmodic intensity are not strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for calm force and the 'talent of Silence' as first characteristics of true greatness. Anti-pattern: men who take convulsion-fits or cannot hold their peace (Rousseau described as intense but not strong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent of Silence
rubrics_metrics.description: The invaluable capacity to remain silent until proper speech or action is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence indicates depth and reserves of strength; many modern/continental figures lack this, undermining their greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnestness / 'In Earnest' Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'heartily in earnest'—sincere, passionate commitment to a cause or truth—is a chief characteristic of a Hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the person's convictions genuinely possess them and drive their actions (Rousseau's earnestness as the first and chief characteristic). Earnestness can be double-edged if combined with weakness of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Egoism / Mastery over Desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Egoism (vanity, hunger for praise) is the source of faults; a Hero should have triumphed over mere desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for signs of vanity, suspicious self-isolation, or petty hunger for applause (anecdotes about Rousseau). These indicate moral weakness undermining heroic stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic Function / Contact with Reality
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hero may function as a Prophet: touching upon reality, declaring an 'awful Reality' rather than abstract sceptical theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the figure communicates truths that move society; even imperfectly expressed prophetic insight (Rousseau's appeals) can have enormous historical effect. Anti-pattern: purely sceptical or merely theoretical voices lacking lived conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary/Aesthetic Genuineness (White Sunlight vs. Rose-Pink)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine literary greatness is 'white sunlight'—depth, universality, and true poetic quality—versus artificial 'rose-pink' operatic sensuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare writers on authenticity and universality: Shakespeare and Goethe as models of true poetic light; Rousseau and many later French writers exemplify artificial prettiness. Use this to judge the literary aspect of a Hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and Truthfulness of Life and Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The song a Hero sings—and the life he lives—must be of a thing really felt; sincerity (a 'great tragic sincerity') is central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authenticity: does the subject express real feeling and truth rather than affectation? Burns exemplifies savage sincerity and truth in both poetry and life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness, Homely Strength, and Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine greatness often rests on robust, original, homely strength—rootedness, vigor, and naturalness rather than artificial polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate temperament and origins (Burns's peasant background) for signs of unpretentious strength, 'rock' quality with wells of softness. Anti-pattern: overly refined, inauthentic mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, Insightful Speech ('having something in it')
rubrics_metrics.description: A great man's speech is notable for always 'having something in it'—concise, illuminating interventions rather than empty loquacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess conversational and rhetorical economy: speaking little but contributing new light on the matter indicates high gift (anecdotes about Burns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Endurance of Prosperity and Adversity (Self-Mastery under Fame)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hero must withstand both adversity and sudden prosperity without becoming inflated or ruined by fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comportment under celebrity: does the person remain tranquil, unastonished, and true to self (Burns in Edinburgh)? Anti-pattern: becoming an 'inflated wind-bag' or being ruined by 'lion-hunters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Destructive Adulation (Lion-hunters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society's sycophants and 'Lion-hunters' who surround and disrupt a Hero's productive life can ruin him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider social environment: excessive attention that hinders work and industry is destructive (Burns's decline after fame). Protective solitude and the ability to work matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingship / The Able-man: Practical Command and Moral Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The King or Able-man embodies the summary of heroism: a commander whose will directs others loyally, combining practical governance with moral/spiritual guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidates for supreme leadership by capacity to command practically and morally: truest-hearted, justest, noblest, whose guidance is the wisest and most fitting for the community. The King has something of the Pontiff; his rule should be obeyed when due.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and Investment of the Able-man
rubrics_metrics.description: Society's task is to find the Ablest Man and invest him with symbols of ability so he can govern according to his faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess social procedures and institutions by how well they discover and empower true ability. Failure to do so (placing a too-unable man in charge) causes systemic collapse and revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine Right vs. Diabolic Wrong in Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim of authority is either rooted in a 'Divine Right' (legitimate moral sanction) or a 'Diabolic Wrong' (illegitimate claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge authorities by moral sanction rather than merely legal or procedural form; claiming obedience without due right or refusing due obedience are both gravely wrong. This is a moral test on rulers and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Ideals and Limits of Realization
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideals (finding a true Able-man, moral perfection) exist and guide action, but cannot be perfectly embodied; a workable approximation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both aspirations and pragmatic realization: demand of institutions a sufficient approximation to ideals (use the plummet/bricklayer metaphor). Too much deviation from foundational standards leads to ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolution as Symptom of Failed Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Social explosions (e.g., French Revolution) often signal the failure to place able, sincere, or morally right men at the head of affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use revolutionary phenomena diagnostically: they often reveal a long-standing loss of moral/truthful government and an urgent need for heroic guidance. They may also have prophetic or purgative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero-worship as Social Solace and Practical Necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in times of doubt and machine-like theories of society, the certainty that Heroes will be sent and that people can reverence them is an enduring social need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural health partly by willingness to recognize and revere genuine greatness; wholesale rejection of authority and heroism risks substituting incompetent leveling ('Liberty and Equality' without authority) that may be disastrous.
